https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/16/four.text: Four years after the death of Mahsa Amini in Iranian police custody, Kurdish businesses across her home region staged a general strike on Wednesday while international human rights organisations warned that those responsible for crushing the 2022 protests remain in power and continue to use the same methods.Shopkeepers and businesses in Saqqez, Sanandaj, Mahabad, Marivan, Baneh and Bokan shut their doors following a call by Kurdish political coalitions. Video circulating on social media showed empty bazaars across the region.Amnesty International, in a report marking the fourth anniversary, said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus.European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (Malta/EPP) said on X that the Parliament would continue to support young Iranians facing execution or imprisonment, singling out the case of twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, sentenced by Tehran's Revolutionary Court after recent protests.The European Parliament "will keep their light shining until it breaks through the darkness.", Metsola wrote on X.UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Iran Mai Sato said that four years of brutal state violence — including lethal force deployed during nationwide protests in late 2025 and early 2026 — have failed to extinguish the resistance."Four years on, the resistance Jina’s death gave rise to has not been extinguished," Sato said in a statement on X."The women and girls who took to the streets in her name still insist on the right to decide what they wear, where they work and how they live... Those rights will not stay deniable forever."Sato also noted that despite the Law on Protecting the Family through the Promotion of the Culture of Chastity and Hijab being formally suspended since December 2024, cafes, restaurants and shops have continued to be closed for hijab violations, with arrests reported in some cases.What happened to Mahsa Amini?Amini, 22, was detained by Tehran's morality police on 13 September 2022 over compulsory hijab rules and died three days later after being brutally beaten in custody.The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran concluded she had been subjected to physical violence in custody and that Iranian authorities were responsible for her death. Iranian officials rejected the findings and denied she had been physically assaulted.Protests spread nationwide in the days after her death. While compulsory hijab and women's rights were central, the movement drew together demands for political freedoms, minority rights, economic justice and changes to the political system.The UN fact-finding mission documented up to 551 deaths across 26 provinces, including at least 49 women and 68 children, and said some violations — including killings, torture, rape and sexual violence — reached the threshold of crimes against humanity.Tehran acknowledged detaining more than 22,000 people, according to Amnesty International, which also documented enforced disappearances, unfair trials and death sentences.Tehran pivots to hi-techCompulsory hijab remains law, the political structure is intact, and many participants in the protests are in prison, in exile or under sentence.The regime has shifted enforcement away from morality-police patrols toward cameras, facial recognition, drones and digital tools. Iran's police announced in 2023 that public cameras would be used to identify women not wearing hijab.The UN fact-finding mission's 2025 report cited facial recognition being used to monitor students' dress at the entrance to Amirkabir University in Tehran.A 2025 study published in the journal Iranian Studies at the University of Cambridge described the movement as producing a "cultural revolution" alongside a political one, arguing it weakened the state's ideological hold over public and cultural life.For instance, images of morality police vans detaining women on the streets were among the most potent symbols of the 2022 protests, prompting Tehran to avoid public confrontation methods.The growing presence of women without headscarves in public spaces and the central place women's rights and freedoms take in political debate show that the situation has not reverted to where it stood before September 2022 — a direct result of the movement's actions.

https://news.ku.edu/news/article/polish-.text: THE UNIVERSITY of KANSAS KU News myKU Email Canvas Enroll & Pay Jayhawk GPS Close News Staff Media Interview Tips KU Communicator Resources Find a KU Faculty Expert When Experts Attack! podcast Hometown News Alerts myKU Email Canvas Enroll & Pay Jayhawk GPS Polish naturalists saved European bison from extinction, research reveals Białowieża National Park in Poland is now home to several hundred European bison, whose restoration from extinction in the wild is the subject of a new research article. Image credit: Nathan Wood Fri, 09/04/2026 author Jon Niccum Share Share by Email Share on LinkedIn Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LAWRENCE — Most people might be surprised to learn that bison are not exclusively found in North America. But as much as the American breed of the large bovine has become a metaphor for callous annihilation and loss, the European breed has experienced an equally volatile saga. “So many people don’t know that there are European bison, and their near-extinction and restoration story, in some respects, is maybe even starker than that of the American bison,” said Nathan Wood, associate professor of history at the University of Kansas. Wood’s new article, titled “Returning ‘Our Royal Animal’ to its ‘Fatherland’: The Near-extinction and Restoration of Bison in Poland after World War I,” reveals this history. He traces how after soldiers and poachers killed the last free European bison, Polish naturalists worked with international organizations to revive the species from the few animals scattered on estates and zoos across the continent. The article appears in Slavic Review. Nathan Wood visited Poland’s Białowieża National Park for his research. “We have these images of the carcasses on the Great Plains of America, with bison getting shot from railway cars and stacks of skulls, and we connect it with ‘taming the West’ and driving out the Plains Indians. But the European bison story is also quite amazing. All living Białowieża bison, which are the lowland ones of today, descend from just seven animals. Now there are more than 1,000 in Białowieża and 10 times that many overall,” Wood said. In some ways, he said, bison became a metaphor for Poland itself. “I wondered, ‘What were Polish patriots thinking when trying to bring back a species from extinction, when they thought of their state as something that had been extinct and brought back to life?” he asked. “They referred to the bison as ‘the royal beast,’ hearkening to the Polish kings that had hunted them. They referred to Białowieża primeval forest as the fatherland. And they referred to Poland as the fatherland, often with a capital F. The resonances of this metonymic relationship were pretty clear for me.” Wood emphasized he is not a large animal biologist, so his contributions to the history of the European bison are based on a pair of conceptual rather than clinical revelations. “I’ve delved into the Polish perspective. What were the people involved in those first two decades of bison restoration in Poland thinking about what they did, and how did they think about the animals they were trying to save?” he said. “The other thing is this parallel between the way that Poles at the time had a ‘civilizing’ mission for the East and how they were trying to civilize the forest and the bison. Other scholarship on European bison restoration has not made this connection.” He said big-city cultural workers for the state were attempting to educate the people in that region because of the assumption they couldn’t be trusted. They predicted the inhabitants — those in the rural east and the people, many of whom would now be considered Belarusians — would poach these animals again, and so it might be too dangerous to reintroduce bison into the forest. Among the most surprising details Wood writes about was a scandal that occurred in 1931. That year, news broke that Prince Hochberg of Pszczyna had permitted Margrave Alfred Wielopolski to shoot two bison on his estate, which threatened to derail the gains Polish authorities had made in reestablishing the animals. “Here the state is hoping to project this image of themselves as, ‘We are civilized, we’re modern, we’re restoring this species.’ And then this prince allows a margrave to come to his estate and pop off two infertile bison. The optics were crazy,” Wood said. Now in his 21st year at KU, Wood specializes in Eastern European history and often teaches courses on World War I. He is on the board of the Polish Institute of Arts and Sciences of America. Wood has lived in Poland numerous times since his early 20s. The professor said he’s spent almost a 10th of his life in the country. “Decades from now, I think there will be more bison in Poland and more in other parts of Europe, too, thanks to contemporary ‘re-wilding’ efforts,” he said. “But conservation projects are always a product of their time. Even if you have the most reputable scientists of the day trying to be involved in the work, you always have to deal with human culture, context, politics and war … or a prince who still sees bison as his property.” Fri, 09/04/2026 author Jon Niccum Media Contacts Jon Niccum KU News Service 785-864-7633 jniccum@ku.edu Share Share by Email Share on LinkedIn Share on Facebook Share on Twitter
